strengths: Identifies concrete, well-explained flaws in the influential AMB algorithm (Xu et al., 2021): improper truncation of Q-updates that breaks the link to historical V-estimates, and a violation of the martingale difference condition in the concentration analysis used to justify optimism/pessimism of the Q-estimators. This is a valuable correction to the literature.

Provides the first fine-grained (individual-gap) regret bound for the widely used UCB-Hoeffding algorithm, improving upon the coarse-grained SA/Δ_min dependence of Yang et al. (2021), and shows the bound matches known lower bounds (Simchowitz & Jamieson 2019; Xu et al. 2021) up to polynomial H factors in favorable regimes.

Introduces a reasonably novel analytical framework that separately tracks optimal vs. suboptimal state-action pairs' visitation/weighted estimation error, which is shown to be broadly applicable (also used for ULCB-Hoeffding).

Proposes two concrete refinements (ULCB-Hoeffding and Refined AMB) that repair AMB's issues, with Refined AMB rigorously proving unbiasedness of the multi-step bootstrapping estimator and re-establishing valid optimism/pessimism guarantees — a nontrivial technical achievement (Theorem G.1 and its lengthy induction proof).

Comprehensive appendix with full proofs, general lemmas, and an explicit technical comparison to model-based fine-grained bounds, clarifying why model-based techniques do not transfer directly to model-free settings.

Empirical results are consistent with the theory (logarithmic growth of regret for corrected algorithms vs. non-flattening regret for original AMB), providing some validation of the corrected analysis.
weaknesses: The H-dependence of the derived bounds (H^5) is substantially worse than the best known model-based fine-grained bounds (H^2 from Chen et al. 2025), and the paper's own comparison (Section C.1) concedes this gap without proposing a path to close it, which somewhat limits the significance of the result.

The core technical innovation (splitting the analysis of optimal vs. suboptimal pairs and using Cauchy-Schwarz separately for each) is a natural extension of existing UCB-regret-analysis machinery (Yang et al. 2021; Zheng et al. 2025b) rather than a conceptually new technique, so the incremental novelty over prior model-free gap-dependent analyses is moderate.

Empirical evaluation is limited to small-scale synthetic tabular MDPs with only 10 trajectories per algorithm and fairly small state/action spaces (largest S=15, A=10, H=10); there is no evaluation on more realistic or larger-scale benchmarks, and no comparison against other advanced UCB-based methods (e.g., UCB-Advantage, Q-EarlySettled-Advantage) despite these being discussed as potential extensions.

The Refined AMB regret bound (Eq. 11) is expressed in terms of |Z_mul| rather than |Z_opt| as in the UCB-based results, and the paper's own simplification (Appendix G.4) shows this bound is essentially never better than a generic SAH^5 bound, raising questions about how much the fine-grained gap-dependence actually buys in the non-UCB setting in practice.

While the identification of AMB's flaws is valuable, the paper does not provide a lower bound example demonstrating that AMB's original (incorrect) guarantee is actually false in practice (only an analytical argument), so the empirical demonstration of AMB's shortcomings could be strengthened.

The presentation is extremely dense and notation-heavy, which may limit accessibility and reproducibility verification by reviewers/readers not deeply familiar with this specific line of work, despite the proofs being complete.

strengths: Identifies concrete, well-substantiated flaws (improper truncation breaking the Q/V recursive link, and violation of the martingale-difference condition in the concentration argument) in the only existing non-UCB-based fine-grained algorithm, AMB (Xu et al., 2021), a published COLT result. This is a meaningful correctness contribution to the literature.

Develops a novel analytical framework that separately tracks visitation/estimation-error contributions of optimal vs. suboptimal state-action pairs, yielding the first fine-grained gap-dependent regret bound for UCB-Hoeffding, a widely used baseline algorithm.
The framework is shown to be general: it is successfully reused to analyze a new UCB-based algorithm (ULCB-Hoeffding), demonstrating flexibility beyond the original target algorithm.

Provides two concrete refinements (ULCB-Hoeffding and Refined AMB) with full, rigorous proofs of optimism/pessimism and unbiasedness of the multi-step bootstrapping estimator (Theorem 4.3), fixing the theoretical gaps identified in AMB.
Regret bounds are shown to match known lower bounds (Simchowitz & Jamieson 2019; Xu et al. 2021) up to polynomial factors in H in relevant regimes, giving confidence in tightness.

Thorough appendix with detailed proofs, auxiliary lemmas, and an insightful comparison to model-based fine-grained results, explaining precisely why model-based analysis techniques do not transfer to the model-free setting.

Empirical results across four scales corroborate the theory (regret curves for the fixed algorithms flatten/grow logarithmically, unlike original AMB), and ULCB-Hoeffding/Refined AMB outperform original AMB, supporting the claimed refinements are practically beneficial.
weaknesses: The final Refined AMB bound (Eq. 11) relies on the coarser |Zmul|/∆min term rather than fully individual gaps ∆h(s,a), so the claimed 'fine-grained' advantage over AMB's original (also |Zmul|-based) bound is more about correctness than tightness improvement.

The H-dependence (H^5) is substantially worse than the state-of-the-art model-based fine-grained bound (H^2 in Chen et al. 2025), and the paper only speculates, without proof, that its framework could improve H-dependence when applied to more advanced model-free algorithms (UCB-Bernstein, UCB-Advantage, etc.).

Empirical evaluation is limited to small synthetic MDPs with randomly generated rewards/transitions (up to H=10, S=15, A=10); no experiments on structured/benchmark environments or larger scale settings, and only 10 trajectories per configuration for uncertainty quantification, which is a fairly modest sample size for reporting percentiles.

The core technical machinery (recursive weighted estimation-error bounds via Cauchy–Schwarz split between optimal/suboptimal pairs) is a natural, if nontrivial, extension of prior techniques (Yang et al. 2021; Zheng et al. 2025b; Zhang et al. 2025a), somewhat limiting the degree of conceptual novelty despite the careful execution.

The presentation is extremely dense with heavy notation (many weight definitions, norms, and recursive quantities), which could hinder accessibility and independent verification by non-specialist readers despite the appendix proofs.

The paper's core distinguishing claim over Yang et al. (2021)/Zheng et al. (2025b) is best realized only in idealized cases (e.g., single suboptimal triple); in the worst case it degrades to match prior coarse-grained results, tempering the practical significance of the improvement.
